```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center", comment = "#>")
# Load the package first (it declares the Python packages it needs), then silence the
# harmless Python warnings about scikit-learn versions to keep the output short.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(epiworldRcalibrate))
reticulate::py_run_string("import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')")
```

This tutorial teaches the package step by step. Every result below was produced by running
the code shown, so you can copy any block and run it yourself.

# What the package does

You have a run of **daily new infections** (we call it a *window*: 30 to 365 days, from the
beginning, middle or end of an epidemic). You know the **population size** `n`, the
**recovery rate** `recov` (1 / the average number of days infectious) and, for the SEIR
model, the **incubation period** `incub` (days). The package estimates:

- **R0**, the basic reproduction number, with a 95% range;
- **ptran** (the transmission probability per contact) and **crate** (contacts per day).
  Only their combination R0 = ptran x crate / recov shapes the curve, so they are reported but
  not separately reliable (section [Estimating ptran and crate](#ptran-crate) shows why);
- **the state on the first day of the window**: the shares of the population exposed (SEIR),
  infectious and recovered;
- **a prediction** of the daily new infections, in the window and after it.

It does this with a **BiLSTM** (a neural network) trained on 1,000,000 simulated epidemics
of the agent-based models `ModelSEIRCONN` and `ModelSIRCONN` from the `epiworldR` package.
The trained networks come with the package: there is nothing to train and no settings to
choose. The package also has:

- four standard methods (ABC-MCMC, ABC-SMC, differential evolution and Nelder-Mead) set up
  the same way, to calibrate with them or compare;
- scores (coverage, interval score) and plots to compare methods;
- real data: COVID-19 cases in US states and Utah, influenza and COVID-19 hospital admissions
  in Utah, and influenza in Baltimore in 1918;
- the functions to train and tune your own BiLSTM.

# Installing

## The R package

From GitHub:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("UofUEpiBio/epiworldRcalibrate")
```

Or from a copy of the code on your computer (a folder with the files `DESCRIPTION`, `R/`,
`inst/`, ...):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_local("path/to/epiworldRcalibrate")
```

or, in a terminal: `R CMD INSTALL path/to/epiworldRcalibrate`. The package is about 50 MB,
because it contains the trained networks. The standard method DE also needs
`install.packages("DEoptim")`.

## Python

The BiLSTM runs in Python (PyTorch), called from R through the `reticulate` package. You do
**not** need to install Python yourself: the first time a BiLSTM is used, `reticulate` sets up
a Python environment with the packages it needs (`numpy`, `pandas`, `torch`, `scikit-learn`,
`joblib`, `optuna`). This takes a few minutes, once.

To use a Python you already have (for example one with a GPU version of PyTorch), tell
`reticulate` where it is **before** loading the package:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "/path/to/python")
library(epiworldRcalibrate)
```

A GPU is used automatically when PyTorch can see one; it is only useful for training. Using
the shipped models is fast on a normal CPU.

## On the CHPC cluster (University of Utah)

```bash
module load R/4.5.2
export RETICULATE_PYTHON=/scratch/general/vast/u1418987/envs/epiworldRcalibrate-gpu/bin/python
Rscript -e 'library(epiworldRcalibrate)'
```

Run long jobs (the standard methods, comparing many windows, training) through SLURM
(`sbatch`), not on the login nodes.

## Check that it works

```{r}
library(epiworldRcalibrate)
packageVersion("epiworldRcalibrate")
window_calibrator("SEIR")
```

Several steps below run in parallel on `CORES` processor cores (forked processes; on Windows
this must be 1):

```{r}
CORES <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") 1L else
  as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK", min(8, parallel::detectCores())))
CORES
```

# Your first calibration

To see how well the method works, we first make a window where we **know the truth**: we run
the SEIR model with chosen values and keep 60 days from the middle of the epidemic.

```{r}
true <- list(n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5, R0 = 2.5, crate = 10)
true$ptran <- true$R0 * true$recov / true$crate

m <- epiworldR::ModelSEIRCONN(name = "example", n = true$n, prevalence = 0.002, contact_rate = true$crate,
                              incubation_days = true$incub, transmission_rate = true$ptran,
                              recovery_rate = true$recov)
epiworldR::verbose_off(m)
epiworldR::run(m, ndays = 150, seed = 42)

# Daily new infectious people: the number moving from Exposed to Infected each day.
tr <- epiworldR::get_hist_transition_matrix(m)
tr <- tr[tr$state_from == "Exposed" & tr$state_to == "Infected", ]
daily <- tr$counts[match(1:150, tr$date)]
daily[is.na(daily)] <- 0

# The true shares in each state at the start of a day, and the true number infectious.
h <- epiworldR::get_hist_total(m)
count_on <- function(day, state) h$counts[h$state == state & h$date == day - 1]
states_at <- function(day) c(exposed_share = count_on(day, "Exposed"), infected_share = count_on(day, "Infected"),
                             recovered_share = count_on(day, "Recovered")) / true$n
infectious <- vapply(1:150, count_on, 0, state = "Infected")

window <- daily[41:100]          # 60 days from the middle of the epidemic
after <- daily[101:114]          # the 14 days after it
plot(daily, type = "h", col = "grey60", xlab = "day", ylab = "new infectious people",
     main = "The simulated epidemic; the window is in blue")
lines(41:100, window, type = "h", col = "#2a78d6")
```

Now we give the window and the known values to the BiLSTM:

```{r}
bilstm <- window_calibrator("SEIR")
fit <- calibrate(window, bilstm, n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5)
fit
```

Against the truth:

```{r}
rbind(truth = c(R0 = true$R0, ptran = true$ptran, crate = true$crate, states_at(41)),
      BiLSTM = calibration_estimate(fit))
```

R0 and the starting state are close. ptran and crate are not, and cannot be: the network only
learns their product (here R0 x recov = `r round(true$R0 * true$recov, 3)`), so it splits it
into a typical ptran and the crate that matches.

To use the numbers in your own code:

```{r}
calibration_estimate(fit)          # all estimates as a named vector
fit$intervals                      # 95% ranges (the BiLSTM gives one for R0)
fit$diagnostics$seconds            # time (the first call also loads Python and the networks)
```

`calibrate()` works the same way for every method in the package: `calibrate(data, method,
known values)`.

# Predicting the curve

`predict_cases()` turns a fit into a 95% band of the daily new infections (and of the number
currently infectious), for the window and `ahead` days after it. There are two ways:

- `method = "simulation"` (the default): run the epiworldR model 500 times from the estimated
  state, with R0 and the state drawn from the fit's uncertainty;
- `method = "renewal"`: the **renewal equation**, the average curve of the same model,
  C_t = R0 x (S_{t-1} / n) x sum_k g_k C_{t-k}, where g is the model's generation interval
  (the time from one infection to the next). It gives almost the same band about 200 times
  faster.

```{r}
band_sim <- predict_cases(fit, ahead = 14)
band_ren <- predict_cases(fit, ahead = 14, method = "renewal")
head(band_sim)
```

`plot_bands()` draws bands side by side: the band and its median, the window (filled points)
and the days after it (open points), with the coverage and interval score of each (next
section):

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
plot_bands(list(`BiLSTM, model runs` = band_sim, `BiLSTM, renewal equation` = band_ren), future = after)
```

The same for the **number currently infectious**, which the BiLSTM never sees (here we know
it because the epidemic is simulated):

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
plot_bands(list(`BiLSTM, model runs` = band_sim, `BiLSTM, renewal equation` = band_ren), what = "infected",
           truth = infectious[41:114])
```

# How good is a prediction?

Two scores compare a band with the values $y_t$ on $T$ days:

- **Coverage**: the share of days inside the band. About 95% is right for a 95% band.
- **Interval score** (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007): on each day the **width of the band**, plus,
  if the value is outside, **40 times the distance to the band**, averaged over the days.
  Lower is better. A band cannot win it just by being wide, and each miss is expensive.

$$\text{IS} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[(u_t - l_t) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l_t - y_t)\mathbf{1}(y_t < l_t) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y_t - u_t)\mathbf{1}(y_t > u_t)\right],\quad \alpha = 0.05.$$

```{r}
interval_score(y = 25, lower = 10, upper = 30)   # inside: the width, 20
interval_score(y = 35, lower = 10, upper = 30)   # 5 above: 20 + 40 x 5 = 220
score_band(band_sim)                             # the window: coverage, width, error of the median, interval score
score_band(band_sim, y = after, days = 61:74)    # the 14 days after the window
```

# Calibrating with the standard methods {#standard}

`window_baselines()` gives four standard methods, set up with the **same unknowns and ranges**
as the BiLSTM: R0 between 0.8 and 5 and the state on the first day of the window. Each fits the
window by running the epiworldR model many times. By default the contact rate is fixed at the
middle of its range (10 for SEIR, 3 for SIR) and ptran = R0 x recov / crate, because only R0
can be learned (the next section searches ptran and crate instead).

| Method | Settings (defaults) | Model runs per window | How it stops |
|---|---|---|---|
| ABC-MCMC | 3,000 random-walk steps (1,500 burn-in) | 3,000 | after 3,000 steps |
| ABC-SMC | 200 particles, 6 generations | up to 30,000 | after 6 generations |
| DE (`DEoptim`) | population 10 x unknowns, 200 generations | 6,000-8,000 | after 200 generations |
| Nelder-Mead (`optim`) | start in the middle of the ranges | 100-500 | when its trial points give the same fit, or after 500 runs |

Each is used like the BiLSTM, with `calibrate()`. One method:

```{r}
baselines <- window_baselines("SEIR")
names(baselines)
fit_smc <- calibrate(window, baselines$`ABC-SMC`, n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5)
fit_smc
```

All four, in parallel (they take minutes each, because they run the model thousands of times):

```{r}
fits <- parallel::mclapply(baselines, function(b) calibrate(window, b, n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5),
                           mc.cores = min(4, CORES))
fits <- c(list(BiLSTM = fit), fits)
summary_table <- t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$estimate[c("R0", "ptran", "crate")], R0_low = f$intervals["R0", 1],
                                              R0_high = f$intervals["R0", 2], seconds = f$diagnostics$seconds,
                                              model_runs = f$diagnostics$model_runs)))
rbind(truth = c(true$R0, true$ptran, true$crate, NA, NA, NA, NA), summary_table)
rbind(truth = states_at(41), t(sapply(fits, function(f) f$estimate[c("exposed_share", "infected_share",
                                                                      "recovered_share")])))
```

The ABC methods give an R0 range (from their posterior); DE and Nelder-Mead give one
estimate. Their bands, with the days after the window:

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
bands <- lapply(fits, predict_cases, ahead = 14)
plot_bands(bands, future = after)
```

And the number currently infectious (not observed by any method):

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
plot_bands(bands, what = "infected", truth = infectious[41:114])
```

To change a setting, give it by method name, for example a longer DE run and a longer chain:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
baselines <- window_baselines("SEIR", settings = list(DE = list(itermax = 400),
                                                      `ABC-MCMC` = list(n_samples = 10000, burnin = 5000)))
```

The help page `?window_baselines` lists every setting.

# Estimating ptran and crate {#ptran-crate}

With `unknowns = "ptran_crate"` the standard methods search ptran (0.0038 to 0.25 for SEIR, on
the log scale) and crate (5 to 15) instead of R0, and R0 = ptran x crate / recov follows. The
ABC methods then give a 95% range for each:

```{r}
free <- window_baselines("SEIR", methods = c("ABC-MCMC", "ABC-SMC"), unknowns = "ptran_crate")
fits_free <- parallel::mclapply(free, function(b) calibrate(window, b, n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5),
                                mc.cores = min(2, CORES))
fits_free$`ABC-SMC`
lapply(fits_free, function(f) signif(f$intervals, 3))   # 95% ranges of R0, ptran and crate
```

The ranges of ptran and crate are wide, while the range of R0 is narrow. `plot_ptran_crate()`
shows why: the accepted values (points) lie along the curve ptran = R0 x recov / crate
(dashed: the estimated R0; orange: the true R0 and the true ptran and crate). Any point on
that curve gives the same epidemic, so the data cannot tell ptran and crate apart:

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=4}
plot_ptran_crate(c(list(BiLSTM = fit), fits_free), truth = c(ptran = true$ptran, crate = true$crate))
```

The BiLSTM gives one ptran (a typical value for the training data) and the crate that matches
its R0; its points show its R0 range. To learn ptran and crate separately, one of them must
come from other data, for example contacts per day from a contact survey.

# Comparing methods on many windows

`compare_methods()` runs every method on every window and scores the predictions. A window is a
list with `cases`, the known values, and optionally the counts after it (`future`), the truth
(`R0`, `ptran`, `crate`, `state`) and labels (such as `position`). Here: windows from the
beginning, middle and end of the simulated epidemic, with the truth.

```{r}
make_window <- function(first, last, position) {
  list(cases = daily[first:last], future = daily[last + 1:14], n = 8000, recov = 1 / 7, incub = 5,
       R0 = true$R0, ptran = true$ptran, crate = true$crate, state = states_at(first), position = position)
}
windows <- list(beginning = make_window(1, 40, "beginning"), middle = make_window(41, 100, "middle"),
                end = make_window(81, 130, "end"))
results <- compare_methods(windows, "SEIR", method = "renewal", cores = CORES)
results[, c("window", "method", "R0", "R0_low", "R0_high", "R0_error", "ptran", "crate", "state_error",
            "coverage", "interval_score", "coverage_ahead", "seconds", "model_runs")]
```

`plot_comparison()` shows the scores by method: a small point per window and a large point for
the mean (blue: the BiLSTM; the orange line marks 95% coverage):

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
plot_comparison(results)
```

`plot_estimates()` shows each method's R0 and 95% range against the truth (orange), window by
window:

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.5}
plot_estimates(results, "R0")
```

# Real data shipped with the package

| Dataset | What it is |
|---|---|
| `covid_us_states` | daily COVID-19 cases in the 50 states and DC, 2020-2023 (Johns Hopkins University), with populations |
| `covid_utah` | daily COVID-19 cases in Utah, 2020-2025 (Utah DHHS) |
| `admissions_utah` | daily influenza and COVID-19 hospital admissions in Utah, 2020-2024 (HHS) |
| `flu_baltimore_1918` | daily influenza cases in Baltimore, 1918 (92 days) |
| `real_data_waves` | the 35 waves of the report, with the known values used for each |

```{r}
head(covid_us_states)
real_data_waves[c(1:3, 31:35), c("wave", "dataset", "start", "end", "n", "recov", "incub")]
```

The counts are reported cases or admissions, not every infection. The report reads them as an
epidemic in a population of `n` people: for US states, cases per 10,000 people with
`n = 10,000`. Known values: COVID-19 `recov` = 1/7 and `incub` = 5 days; influenza `recov` =
0.25 and `incub` = 2 days. `wave_data()` gives the counts of one wave:

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.5}
ny <- wave_data("New York Omicron 2021-22")
plot(ny$time, ny$count, type = "h", col = "grey50", xlab = "", ylab = "cases per 10,000 people",
     main = "New York, Omicron wave")
```

## Baltimore, 1918

```{r}
baltimore <- flu_baltimore_1918$cases
fit_seir <- calibrate(baltimore[1:60], window_calibrator("SEIR"), n = 10000, recov = 0.25, incub = 2)
fit_sir  <- calibrate(baltimore[1:60], window_calibrator("SIR"), n = 10000, recov = 0.25)
fit_seir
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
plot_bands(list(`BiLSTM, SEIR` = predict_cases(fit_seir, ahead = 14), `BiLSTM, SIR` = predict_cases(fit_sir, ahead = 14)),
           future = baltimore[61:74])
```

Real reported cases have more noise than the simulations the BiLSTM was trained on (weekday
effects, reporting delays, spikes), so the band misses some days.

## Windows of real data

`real_data_windows()` cuts windows from the beginning, the middle (around the peak) and the
end of the waves, ready for `calibrate()` and `compare_methods()`. With the defaults it gives
the report's 315 windows (lengths 30, 60 and 90 days). Here: the 9 windows of the New York
Omicron wave, with the BiLSTM, ABC-MCMC and Nelder-Mead:

```{r}
ny_windows <- real_data_windows("New York Omicron 2021-22")
length(ny_windows)
str(ny_windows[[1]][c("n", "recov", "incub", "wave", "position")])
real_results <- compare_methods(ny_windows, "SEIR",
                                calibrators = c(list(BiLSTM = bilstm),
                                                window_baselines("SEIR", methods = c("ABC-MCMC", "NelderMead"))),
                                cores = CORES)
aggregate(cbind(R0, coverage, interval_score, coverage_ahead, seconds) ~ method, real_results, mean)
```

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.5}
plot_comparison(real_results, measures = c("coverage", "interval_score", "coverage_ahead", "seconds"), ncol = 4)
```

On this wave ABC-MCMC, which fits each window directly with wide bands, covers the observed
days better than the BiLSTM. Over all 270 SEIR windows from US states in the report, the
BiLSTM covered 94% of the days and ABC-MCMC 98%; real case reports have weekday effects and
spikes that the noise-free training epidemics do not have.

For all the real-data windows (this takes several hours on one core, so use many cores or a
cluster):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
all_windows <- real_data_windows()
all_results <- compare_methods(all_windows, "SEIR", cores = 32)
```

# Making your own BiLSTM

The shipped models cover `n` from 5,000 to 10,000, `recov` from 0.071 to 0.25, `incub` from 1
to 21 days (SEIR), crate from 5 to 15 (SEIR) or 1 to 5 (SIR), and R0 from 0.8 to 5. For other
ranges, train your own in three steps:

1. **Simulate** training epidemics: `simulate_window_data()`;
2. **Tune** the network settings (optional): `tune_window_calibrator()`;
3. **Train** the networks: `train_window_calibrator()`, then use them with
   `window_calibrator(model_dir = ...)`.

Below everything is tiny, so it runs in a few minutes on a laptop; the numbers it gives are
not meaningful. The real settings are in the table after the code.

```{r}
folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "my_model")
data <- simulate_window_data("SIR", n_sims = 600, output_dir = file.path(folder, "data"), n_days = 120,
                             priors = list(R0 = c(1, 3)), cores = CORES)
best <- tune_window_calibrator(data, output_dir = file.path(folder, "tuning"), n_trials = 2, epochs = 2,
                               subset = 400, device = "cpu")
best
train_window_calibrator(data, output_dir = file.path(folder, "model"), seeds = 1:2, hyperparameters = best,
                        epochs = 3, n_calib = 600, device = "cpu", cores = CORES)
my_bilstm <- window_calibrator("SIR", model_dir = file.path(folder, "model"), k = 50)
calibrate(baltimore[1:60], my_bilstm, n = 10000, recov = 0.25)
```

| Step | Tiny version above | The shipped models |
|---|---|---|
| `simulate_window_data()` | 600 epidemics of 120 days | 1,000,000 epidemics of 365 days (about 2 hours on 32 cores for SEIR) |
| `tune_window_calibrator()` | 2 trials of 2 epochs | 40 trials of 20 epochs on 100,000 epidemics (a few GPU hours) |
| `train_window_calibrator()` | 2 networks, 3 epochs | 5 networks, 50 epochs (about 4 hours per SEIR network on a recent GPU) |

Training uses a GPU when one is available (`device = "auto"`); with `resume = TRUE` (the
default) a run that stops continues from its last epoch.

# Rendering documents

**This tutorial** is the file `TUTORIAL.Rmd` in the package folder. To make the HTML page:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rmarkdown::render("TUTORIAL.Rmd")          # writes TUTORIAL.html next to it
```

or in a terminal: `Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("TUTORIAL.Rmd")'`. In RStudio or VS Code, open
the file and click *Knit*. It takes about 45 minutes on 16 cores, mostly for the standard methods.

**The report** with all the results (`examples/results/report/Report_SEIR_SIR.html`) is made by
`examples/Report_SEIR_SIR.Rmd` from the saved results of the other files in `examples/`; the
order is in `examples/README.md`. Each results folder has a `logs/` folder with the SLURM
scripts used on CHPC, for example:

```bash
cd examples/results/report && sbatch logs/report.sbatch
```

**The package documentation**: the help pages (`?window_calibrator`, `?predict_cases`, ...),
the vignette `vignette("Window_calibration")`, and a website with all of them:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
pkgdown::build_site()                      # writes the website to docs/
```

# When something goes wrong

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| `Python ... not found` or `No module named torch` | Let `reticulate` install Python (restart R and load the package), or set `RETICULATE_PYTHON` to a Python that has `torch`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `joblib` (and `optuna` for tuning) before `library(epiworldRcalibrate)`. |
| Warnings about scikit-learn versions | Harmless: the networks' scalers were saved with another version. |
| The first `calibrate()` takes 10-20 seconds | Loading Python and the networks; the next calls take a fraction of a second. |
| `DE needs the package 'DEoptim'` | `install.packages("DEoptim")`. |
| ABC-SMC stops with "exhausted its ... budget" | Give it more runs: `window_baselines(settings = list(`ABC-SMC` = list(sim_budget = 60000)))`. |
| Values outside the training ranges (for example `n` = 1,000,000) | Scale the counts to a population the models know (for example cases per 10,000 people with `n = 10000`), or train your own model. |
| `mclapply` hangs or errors on Windows | Use `cores = 1` (forked processes are not available on Windows). |

# All functions and data

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `window_calibrator(model)` | the trained BiLSTM for SEIR or SIR windows |
| `window_baselines(model, unknowns)` | ABC-MCMC, ABC-SMC, DE and Nelder-Mead, set up the same way; `unknowns = "ptran_crate"` searches ptran and crate |
| `calibrate(cases, method, ...)` | fit a window; known values `n`, `recov` (and `incub` for SEIR) |
| `calibration_estimate(fit)` | the estimates as a named vector |
| `predict_cases(fit, ahead, method)` | 95% bands by model runs or the renewal equation |
| `coverage()`, `interval_score()`, `score_band()` | how well a band matches the data |
| `compare_methods(windows, model)` | all methods on many windows |
| `plot_bands()`, `plot_comparison()`, `plot_estimates()`, `plot_ptran_crate()` | plots to compare methods |
| `wave_data()`, `real_data_windows()` | the counts of a real wave; windows of real data |
| `covid_us_states`, `covid_utah`, `admissions_utah`, `flu_baltimore_1918`, `real_data_waves` | real data |
| `simulate_window_data()`, `tune_window_calibrator()`, `train_window_calibrator()` | make your own BiLSTM |

The package's general tools (simulators, other calibrators, `make_calibrator()`,
`compare_calibrators()`) are described in `vignette("Getting_started")`.

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```
